propositions.text: The appellants Vidéotron Ltée and Groupe TVA inc. appeal the Federal Court summary trial judgment by Justice Grammond on February 24, 2022.

The Judge held respondent companies Technologies Konek inc. and Coopérative de câblodistribution Hill Valley jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmission of Groupe TVA stations.
The Judge exonerated respondent company Libéo inc. from liability relating to the infringements at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states appellants Vidéotron and Groupe TVA appeal a Federal Court judgment holding Konek and Hill Valley liable for copyright infringements but exonerating Libéo.

propositions.text: Appellants ask the Court to find Libéo jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements due to direct involvement.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue Libéo should be held jointly liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements due to direct involvement.

propositions.text: Having reviewed the record and arguments, the Court would allow the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court would allow the appeal after reviewing the record and arguments.

propositions.text: The Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17 of his decision, which are reproduced as relevant for this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Judge summarized the facts at paragraphs 8–17, which are reproduced here for the appeal.

propositions.text: Appellant TVA Group is a Canadian television broadcaster owning TVA and TVA Sports stations.
Appellant Vidéotron is a broadcasting distribution undertaking (BDU) that retransmits TVA and TVA Sports stations to subscribers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states TVA Group owns TVA stations and Vidéotron is a BDU retransmitting those stations to subscribers.

propositions.text: Respondent Libéo, founded in 1996, operates in IT and website hosting; Jean-François Rousseau was CEO until 2019, Joé Bussière president since 2016.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Libéo as an IT company founded in 1996 with Rousseau as CEO until 2019 and Bussière as president since 2016.

propositions.text: In 2016, Rousseau partnered with Louis Michaud to form Konek Technologies Inc. to design technological solutions for hotels.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau and Michaud formed Konek Technologies in 2016 to design hotel technological solutions.

propositions.text: In 2018, Konek designed the 'Konek box' under contract with Libéo, enabling hotel TVs to retransmit various stations.
Rousseau gradually disengaged from Libéo and left CEO position in 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Konek designed the 'Konek box' for Libéo in 2018 and Rousseau left Libéo's CEO role in 2019.

propositions.text: In February 2020, Rousseau helped form Hill Valley to provide more TV stations to hotels subscribing to Konek's services.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Rousseau formed Hill Valley in 2020 to expand TV station offerings to Konek's hotel subscribers.

propositions.text: Hill Valley applied to CRTC on December 30, 2020, for BDU exemption; CRTC approved on February 3, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Hill Valley applied for and received CRTC BDU exemption between December 2020 and February 2021.

propositions.text: Vidéotron discovered Konek's retransmission activities in 2020 and confirmed retransmission of TVA stations via internet in hotel rooms.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Vidéotron found Konek retransmitting TVA stations via internet in hotels in 2020.

propositions.text: On February 26, 2021, appellants sued Konek, Hill Valley, Libéo and their directing minds for copyright infringement by unauthorized retransmission.
On same day, Vidéotron terminated service contract with Libéo for decoders used to retransmit TVA stations.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants sued the respondents and their directors for copyright infringement and terminated Libéo's service contract on February 26, 2021.

propositions.text: The Judge set out summary trial framework and agreed with parties to proceed by summary trial under rule 216 Federal Courts Rules.
Parties agreed directors’ liability issue would not be decided at summary trial; debate limited to corporate entities Konek, Libéo, Hill Valley.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge proceeded by summary trial on corporate entities only, excluding directors’ liability, under rule 216.

propositions.text: Appellants argued Konek, Libéo, Hill Valley infringed copyright by retransmitting TVA stations.
Respondents argued retransmission was exempt under section 31 of the Copyright Act, so no infringement occurred.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argued infringement by retransmission; respondents claimed exemption under section 31 of Copyright Act.

propositions.text: Retransmission of TVA Sports not covered by section 31 exemption (paras. 45, 100).
Before Feb 3, 2021, Konek and Hill Valley not 'retransmitters' under section 31, so no exemption for TVA retransmission (paras. 53–54, 100).
Konek and Hill Valley jointly and severally liable for copyright infringements in retransmission not covered by section 31 exemption (paras. 95, 101).

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found TVA Sports retransmission not exempt, Konek and Hill Valley not retransmitters before Feb 3, 2021, and liable for infringements.

propositions.text: Judge found Konek and Hill Valley jointly liable for copyright infringements when retransmissions not exempt under section 31.
Judge found Libéo not liable for infringements committed by Konek and Hill Valley.
Appellants challenge Judge’s finding exonerating Libéo from liability for retransmissions.

paragraphs.summary: The Judge found Konek and Hill Valley liable but exonerated Libéo; appellants challenge Libéo’s exoneration.

propositions.text: Court allowed Mr. Spicer to make brief representations on subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) of the Copyright Act despite not appearing on record.
Subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) are not at issue in this appeal; no ruling needed on their scope.

paragraphs.summary: The court allowed brief representations on subsections 27(2.3) and 27(2.4) but these are not at issue in this appeal.

propositions.text: Standard of review from Housen v. Nikolaisen: correctness for questions of law, palpable and overriding error for fact or mixed fact and law.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is correctness for law and palpable error for fact or mixed questions per Housen.

propositions.text: Issue is whether Judge erred in applying legal principles and correctly identified legal framework for analysis.
If trial judge uses wrong legal principle, no deference is owed (citing Canada (Commissioner of Official Languages) v. Canada (Employment and Social Development)).

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as whether the Judge erred legally, noting no deference if wrong legal principle applied.

propositions.text: It is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in Canada to many programs broadcast on TVA and TVA Sports stations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it is undisputed that Groupe TVA owns copyright in programs broadcast on TVA stations.

propositions.text: Subsection 3(1) of the CA grants Groupe TVA the sole right to communicate its programs to the public by telecommunication.

paragraphs.summary: The court states subsection 3(1) of the CA grants Groupe TVA the sole right to communicate its programs by telecommunication.

propositions.text: CCH confirms subsection 3(1) includes the right to authorize acts and defines authorization as approval or sanction, which can be inferred from acts or indifference.
Authorization can be inferred from acts less than direct and positive, including indifference, but not mere provision of equipment.
Courts presume authorization is only lawful.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains CCH defines authorization as approval inferred from acts or indifference, excluding mere equipment use, with a presumption of lawful authorization.

propositions.text: The presumption of authorization may be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between authorizer and infringers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the presumption of authorization can be rebutted by showing a relationship or control between authorizer and infringers.

propositions.text: CCH does not require a particular legal relationship to rebut the presumption of authorization; other circumstances suffice.

paragraphs.summary: The court states CCH allows rebutting authorization presumption without a particular legal relationship.

propositions.text: Paragraph 2.4(1)(b) of the CA excludes from communication those who only provide telecommunication means for others to communicate.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains paragraph 2.4(1)(b) excludes from communication those only providing telecommunication means for others.

propositions.text: SOCAN and Lackman interpret paragraph 2.4(1)(b) to protect intermediaries acting as conduits without knowledge or influence over content.

paragraphs.summary: The court states SOCAN and Lackman interpret paragraph 2.4(1)(b) to protect intermediaries acting as conduits without content knowledge or influence.

propositions.text: Paragraph 31.1(1) of the CA exempts providers of Internet-related services from copyright infringement solely for providing telecommunication or reproduction means.

paragraphs.summary: The court states paragraph 31.1(1) exempts Internet service providers from copyright infringement for providing telecommunication means.

propositions.text: The Judge erred in requiring proof of fraud, abuse of right or public order contravention to lift Libéo's corporate veil.
Lifting the corporate veil was not an issue the Judge had to decide, so proof was not required.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the Judge erred by requiring proof to lift Libéo's corporate veil, which was not an issue to decide.

propositions.text: Libéo argues the Judge did not err given the evidence at summary trial.
Respondents criticize the Judge for ruling on issues not submitted, including Hill Valley's BDU qualification periods.
No cross-appeal was filed on Hill Valley's BDU issue, so the Court will not address it.

paragraphs.summary: Libéo argues no error; respondents criticize Judge ruling on unsubmitted issues; court declines to address unappealed issue.

propositions.text: Appellants insist lifting Libéo's corporate veil was not submitted to the Judge and proof was not required.
Libéo concedes appellants did not refer to corporate veil but Judge applied principle due to inseparability argument.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants insist corporate veil was not submitted; Libéo concedes Judge applied it due to inseparability argument.

propositions.text: Parties' trial memoranda confirm corporate veil was not raised as an issue.
Judge understood appellants' position that Konek and Hill Valley are one and the same and Libéo liable for leasing decoders used to retransmit TVA.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties did not raise corporate veil; Judge understood appellants claimed Konek and Hill Valley are one and same and Libéo liable.

propositions.text: Judge addressed Libéo's liability by examining lifting corporate veil and distinct corporate personality.
Judge found no basis to lift Libéo's corporate veil due to lack of fraud, abuse of right or public order contravention.
Close ties or website statement do not override distinct legal personalities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Judge examined corporate veil and found no basis to lift it due to lack of fraud or abuse, despite close ties.

propositions.text: Appellants did not allege Libéo liable through lifting corporate veil but for direct copyright infringement by telecommunication.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Libéo liable for direct copyright infringement, not via lifting corporate veil.

propositions.text: Judge applied incorrect legal framework focusing on fault of another via corporate veil, not Libéo's direct fault.
Judge erred by seeking evidence of fraud or abuse to lift veil when direct fault was sole issue.
Judge should have asked parties for submissions if concerned about corporate veil but did not.
Judge must decide issues based on record and arguments submitted (CXS Transportation).

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Judge erred applying corporate veil framework instead of direct fault, should have sought submissions, and decide on submitted record.

propositions.text: Had Judge used correct legal framework, he would have found Libéo liable for copyright infringement.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants conclude Judge would have found Libéo liable if correct legal framework applied.

propositions.text: Judge relied on Rousseau's testimony that Konek paid decoder costs and Bussière's unawareness to disregard Libéo's liability.
Judge found presence of decoders in Libéo's server room insufficient to hold Libéo liable without evidence of awareness.
Judge found same individual heading both companies insufficient to treat corporations as one.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Judge relied on testimony and lack of awareness to dismiss Libéo's liability despite decoders in its server room.

propositions.text: All evidence contradicts Judge's finding when analyzed under correct legal framework.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue all evidence contradicts Judge's finding under correct legal framework.

propositions.text: Rousseau and Bussière have long business relationship and overlapping roles in Libéo and Konek.
Rousseau founded Libéo in 1996, was president and CEO until 2019, remains majority shareholder with ultimate control.
Bussière replaced Rousseau as president in 2016 and is second largest shareholder; Libéo is small business with two directors.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Rousseau and Bussière's overlapping roles and control in Libéo and Konek, with Rousseau as founder and majority shareholder.

propositions.text: Konek was co-founded by Bussière and Rousseau, who are equal shareholders and directors.
Konek provides integrated TV and internet services for hotels, including TVA stations via Konek boxes.
Konek shared premises with Libéo until 2019 and remains adjacent to Libéo's location.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Konek was co-founded by Bussière and Rousseau, provides hotel TV services including TVA, and shared premises with Libéo.

propositions.text: Libéo played important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure including encoding servers.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Libéo's important role in Konek after 2018 contract, knowing Konek would use its infrastructure.

propositions.text: Libéo was involved in developing Konek's infrastructure after signing the contract.
Libéo designed and supplied 'Konek boxes'.
Libéo developed software for the Konek boxes.
Libéo provided infrastructure and servers to operate Konek services, including encoding capture servers.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Libéo developed Konek's infrastructure, designed and supplied Konek boxes, developed software for them, and provided servers.

propositions.text: In August 2019, Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron television services.
Joé Bussière confirmed a Vidéotron technician accessed Libéo's secure room during ILLICO decoder installation.
A Libéo director knew the server room contained ILLICO terminals.
Jean-François Rousseau personally gave Vidéotron technician access to Libéo server room and still had access as of Sept 27, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron services; witnesses confirmed Vidéotron technician accessed Libéo's server room containing ILLICO terminals.

propositions.text: Some ILLICO decoders hosted by Libéo were tuned to TVA Sports and retransmitted to hotels.
Respondents claim Konek paid for ILLICO decoders, so Libéo did not retransmit TVA content and is not liable.
This argument is without merit; Libéo was responsible for use of rented ILLICO decoders on its premises.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondents' claim that Libéo was not liable for retransmission is without merit; Libéo was responsible for decoders' use.

propositions.text: A document from Libéo's website describes a partnership and alliance with Konek and highlights Libéo's innovation role.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a Libéo website document showing a partnership and alliance with Konek and Libéo's innovation role.

propositions.text: Given evidence, it is difficult to find Libéo unaware of decoder use and not actively participating in communicating TVA programs.
Libéo subscribed to Vidéotron services via ILLICO decoders, receives and illegally retransmits TVA signals through Konek's services.
Libéo is directly participating and cannot claim exemptions under the CA.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Libéo directly participated in illegal retransmission of TVA signals and cannot claim CA exemptions.

propositions.text: Appellants submit Judge erred by not ordering permanent injunction against Konek and Hill Valley after finding section 31 CA did not apply.
Appellants do not ask Court to decide injunction issue separately but to address it obiter due to unclear case law on summary trials.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue the Judge erred by not ordering a permanent injunction and ask the Court to address this issue obiter.

propositions.text: Court finds it inappropriate to address injunction issue abstractly as it was resubmitted to Judge at trial.
Judge held Konek and Hill Valley liable for copyright infringements but declined injunction due to agreement on summary trial scope.
Appellants face summary judgment without practical effect and must incur further costs for injunction issue later.
This result appears contrary to proportionality and sound administration of justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to address injunction issue now, noting appellants face further costs and the result seems unjust.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed, judgment set aside in part with costs, and judgment rendered holding Libéo liable for copyright infringements.
Libéo is jointly and severally liable with Konek and Hill Valley for copyright infringements.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside part of the judgment, and holds Libéo jointly liable for copyright infringements.
